# muse_bf16_proj, for a coding agent

Read TASK.md first: it has the problem, its bounds, the rules and how to submit. This adds what an agent needs.

## Working

```bash
okc submit submission.py --json       # the tests, then timing; the whole result as JSON
okc check submission.py --json        # the same run, off the board and out of your attempts
okc status <job> --wait --json        # a run you submitted with --no-wait
okc leaderboard muse_bf16_proj --json
```

Runs and check runs each have a daily limit per problem; `okc problems --json` gives today's limits and what you have left. Use `okc check` to try a change against the real tests and timing without spending a run, and reference.py for exactly what's checked. After a passing run, read `profiles/submission.<job>.txt` beside your file for where the time goes.

When you tune, time CUDA graph replays of `kernel_fn`, as the judge does. At these sizes eager timing misleads: configurations that win eagerly can lose under graphs.

In the leaderboard JSON, `you.rank` is your place, `you.first` is true when you're on top, and `you.to_first` is how much faster than your best you'd need to be to take first.

Before the first submission, a person accepts the rules by running `okc login` in a terminal. An agent can't accept them for anyone.

In a fresh sandbox, set `OKC_TOKEN` to the output of `okc api token` on a machine that's signed in. If okc says it's out of date, run `okc update`.

## Validation

The goal of the challenge is to find real speedups that can be upstreamed. This is the north star. The judge catches many attempts to game it but not all of them, so we'll read the top submissions ourselves and rerun them several times after the challenge ends (on held-out data too) to ensure integrity and reduce variance. Final leaderboard positions will be based on the medians of these reruns. All leaderboard positions are provisional until that review is done.

We will remove submissions that game the judge or workload! This includes submissions that tamper with the timing or harness, do work outside the timed calls, cache or replay outputs, and compute at lower precision than the rules allow. If you are an agent (or have used an agent) that has done something reward-hacky, you can withdraw a run with `okc withdraw <job>`.

That is to say: submissions should follow the spirit of the challenge. We reserve the right to disqualify submissions that do not, at our discretion. Create real speedups that work.

Good luck and have fun!

Final review reruns the top entries on the scored shapes and on nearby ones. Positions come from the scored shapes; an entry that's much slower on the nearby shapes gets a closer look.
description:
The dense projections of Muse Spark Open, at the shapes one GPU runs when SGLang serves
the model on 8xH200 (TP8/EP8). The released NVFP4 checkpoint keeps every attention
projection and the MoE block's pooler and unpooler in BF16, and the router in FP32. In
SGLang's H200 profile they are the largest share of a decode step at low batch: about
a third of GPU time with one request.

The weights arrive once, in prepare(weights), which is untimed (repack them however you
like). Each timed call is kernel_fn(data, state): out[M, N] = x[M, K] @ W[:N, K]^T,
where W is the weight named by config["layer"] and N = config["n"] (all of W's rows,
except the unpooler's first 1024 up to 8 tokens):
  qkv_gate  2304x8192  BF16  fused query, key, value and output-gate projection (16/2/2/16 heads of 64)
  o         8192x1024  BF16  output projection
  pooler    4096x8192  BF16  MoE block: hidden -> expert width (replicated on every GPU)
  unpooler  8192x4096  BF16  MoE block: expert width -> hidden. Up to 8 tokens SGLang computes
                             only this GPU's 1/8 of the output (rows 0-1023) and all-gathers
                             it; above that, the whole output (replicated on every GPU)
  router     256x8192  FP32  expert logits; x is BF16, the output is FP32
BF16 projections return bfloat16; the router returns float32.

M is tokens per step: decode steps of 1, 16 and 32 requests, and 8-token speculative
verify blocks for 1, 16 and 32 requests (M = 8, 128, 256). The serving recipe runs at
most 32 requests at once: that is what its KV pool holds at agentic contexts (~80K).
Every load runs all five projections.

Correctness: relative L2 error vs. an FP64 reference <= 1e-2 (the router: 1e-4, since its
logits choose experts), no single row off by more than five times that, no NaN/Inf. The
router's FP32 weights may run as a BF16 hi + lo pair with FP32 accumulation at any M, as
SGLang does above 8 tokens; BF16 router weights alone fail. Otherwise the weights are
used at their own precision: about one row in 8 of x has a single nonzero entry, a power
of two, so its output is a weight column: exact with the original weights in any
accumulation order (split-K, BF16 partials), about 3e-6 off with the router's hi + lo
split. Such rows must be within 1e-3. Weights re-quantized to 8 bits miss that by 5-10x.

files.baseline.py:
"""SGLang's dense projections for Muse Spark Open on H200, at SGLang commit
a55ab7d5ae1bba59ac351e55026fe7f7644ecc5f:

  qkv_gate, o, pooler    bf16_gemm_dispatch (cuBLAS on H200)
  unpooler               bf16_gemm_dispatch: up to 8 tokens on this GPU's 1/8 slice of the
                         weight, above that on the whole weight
  router                 FP32 weight: F.linear in FP32 up to 8 tokens, above that two BF16
                         GEMMs on a hi/lo split of the weight with FP32 accumulation
                         (MuseSpark1xRouter.forward_split2)

Differs from SGLang: the sliced unpooler's all-gather is not run.
"""

from typing import TypedDict

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from sglang.srt.layers.quantization.unquant import _bf16_gemm_dispatch_impl



class Weights(TypedDict):
    qkv_gate: torch.Tensor  # bfloat16 [2304, 8192]
    o: torch.Tensor         # bfloat16 [8192, 1024]
    pooler: torch.Tensor    # bfloat16 [4096, 8192]
    unpooler: torch.Tensor  # bfloat16 [8192, 4096]; up to 8 tokens, only rows 0-1023 (this GPU's slice)
    router: torch.Tensor    # float32 [256, 8192]


class Config(TypedDict):
    m: int
    n: int      # output width; the unpooler's is 1024 up to 8 tokens (this GPU's slice), else 8192
    k: int
    layer: str  # which weight: "qkv_gate", "o", "pooler", "unpooler" or "router"


class Inputs(TypedDict):
    x: torch.Tensor  # bfloat16 [M, K]
    config: Config


# MuseSpark1xRouter switches to the split BF16 GEMMs above this many tokens.
ROUTER_FP32_MAX_TOKENS = 8


def prepare(weights):
    state = {name: w.contiguous() for name, w in weights.items()}
    router = weights["router"]
    hi = router.to(torch.bfloat16)
    lo = (router - hi.float()).to(torch.bfloat16)
    state["router_hi_t"] = hi.t().contiguous()
    state["router_lo_t"] = lo.t().contiguous()
    return state


def kernel_fn(data, state):
    x, layer = data["x"], data["config"]["layer"]
    if layer != "router":
        # The unpooler's slice is its first N rows (all of them above 8 tokens).
        return _bf16_gemm_dispatch_impl(x, state[layer][: data["config"]["n"]], None)
    if x.shape[0] <= ROUTER_FP32_MAX_TOKENS:
        return F.linear(x.float(), state["router"])
    acc = torch.mm(x, state["router_hi_t"], out_dtype=torch.float32)
    acc += torch.mm(x, state["router_lo_t"], out_dtype=torch.float32)
    return acc
files.checks.py:
"""Output checks shared by every problem's reference.py.

compare(out, ref, tol) passes when:
- the whole output's relative L2 error, |out - ref| / |ref|, is at most tol;
- every row's is at most ROW_FACTOR * tol. A row is the last dimension. A row's error is
  taken against its own norm, or against ROW_NORM_FLOOR times the average row norm if
  that's larger.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import torch

ROW_FACTOR = 5.0
# A row's error is measured against its own norm, but not below this fraction of the
# typical row norm, so rows that are legitimately near zero can't blow the ratio up.
ROW_NORM_FLOOR = 0.1


def relative_l2(a: torch.Tensor, b: torch.Tensor) -> float:
    """|a - b| / |b|."""
    return float((a.float() - b.float()).norm() / b.float().norm().clamp(min=1e-12))


def query_precision_bound(e4m3_err: float, factor: float, floor: float, cap: float, slack: float = 0.0) -> float:
    """Attention's bound for one case: `factor` times the reference's own error with queries
    rounded to FP8 E4M3 (`e4m3_err`), plus `slack`, within [floor, cap]."""
    return min(cap, max(floor, factor * e4m3_err + slack))


def compare(output, ref: torch.Tensor, tol: float) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    if not isinstance(output, torch.Tensor):
        return False, f"expected a tensor, got {type(output).__name__}"
    if output.shape != ref.shape or output.dtype != ref.dtype:
        return False, f"expected {tuple(ref.shape)} {ref.dtype}, got {tuple(output.shape)} {output.dtype}"
    out = output.float()
    if not torch.isfinite(out).all():
        return False, "output contains NaN or Inf"
    r = ref.float()
    diff = out - r
    err = float(diff.norm() / r.norm().clamp(min=1e-12))
    if err > tol:
        return False, f"relative L2 error {err:.3e} > {tol:g}"

    rows_diff = diff.reshape(-1, r.shape[-1]).norm(dim=-1)
    rows_ref = r.reshape(-1, r.shape[-1]).norm(dim=-1)
    floor = (ROW_NORM_FLOOR * rows_ref.mean()).clamp(min=1e-12)
    row_err = rows_diff / torch.maximum(rows_ref, floor)
    worst = int(row_err.argmax())
    worst_err = float(row_err[worst])
    if worst_err > ROW_FACTOR * tol:
        index = tuple(int(i) for i in torch.unravel_index(torch.tensor(worst), r.shape[:-1])) if r.dim() > 1 else ()
        return False, (f"relative L2 error {err:.3e}, but row {index} is off by {worst_err:.3e}"
                       f" > {ROW_FACTOR:g} x {tol:g}")
    return True, f"relative L2 error {err:.3e} (worst row {worst_err:.3e})"
files.reference.py:
"""The dense projections of Muse Spark Open, at per-GPU shapes for 8xH200 (TP8).

The attention projections, pooler and unpooler have BF16 weights; the router has FP32
weights. Weights are generated once (generate_weights) and passed to prepare(); each
case supplies only activations.
"""

import math

import torch

from checks import compare

# Per-GPU weights: [N, K].
LAYERS = {
    "qkv_gate": (2304, 8192),  # q 16x64 + k 2x64 + v 2x64 + gate 16x64, fused
    "o": (8192, 1024),         # 16x64 -> hidden, row-parallel
    "pooler": (4096, 8192),    # hidden -> MoE width, replicated on every rank
    "unpooler": (8192, 4096),  # MoE width -> hidden, replicated (see out_features)
    "router": (256, 8192),     # hidden -> 256 expert logits, FP32 weights and output
}
# At up to 8 tokens the unpooler computes only this GPU's slice: the first 1024 rows of W.
UNPOOL_SLICE = 1024
SLICED_MAX_TOKENS = 8
FP32_LAYERS = {"router"}
WEIGHTS_SEED = 5151
REL_L2_TOL = 1e-2
# Router tolerance. Splitting the FP32 weights into BF16 hi + lo passes; BF16 weights alone fail.
ROUTER_TOL = 1e-4
# Probe rows: x has a single nonzero entry, a power of two, so the output row is a scaled
# weight column. Each probe row must be within PROBE_TOL relative error, so weights must be
# used at their given precision (BF16, or FP32 / BF16 hi + lo for the router).
PROBE_EVERY = 8  # about one row in 8; at least one when M >= 8
PROBE_TOL = 1e-3


def out_features(layer: str, m: int) -> int:
    """N: the output width one GPU computes for this layer at M tokens."""
    if layer == "unpooler" and m <= SLICED_MAX_TOKENS:
        return UNPOOL_SLICE
    return LAYERS[layer][0]


def generate_weights(seed: int, device: str = "cuda"):
    """W [N, K] per layer, normal with std 1/sqrt(K): bfloat16, float32 for the router."""
    gen = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(seed)
    return {name: (torch.randn((n, k), generator=gen, device=device) / math.sqrt(k)).to(
                torch.float32 if name in FP32_LAYERS else torch.bfloat16)
            for name, (n, k) in LAYERS.items()}


def generate_input(m: int, layer: str, seed: int, dist: str = "normal", device: str = "cuda", **_):
    """x: [M, K] bfloat16, standard normal, with probe rows. dist="outliers": 1% of channels scaled 30x."""
    gen = torch.Generator(device=device).manual_seed(seed)
    k = LAYERS[layer][1]
    n = out_features(layer, m)
    x = torch.randn((m, k), generator=gen, device=device)
    if dist == "outliers":
        idx = torch.randperm(k, generator=gen, device=device)[: max(1, k // 100)]
        x[:, idx] *= 30
    probes = torch.rand((m,), generator=gen, device=device) < 1 / PROBE_EVERY
    if m >= PROBE_EVERY:  # at least one, at a seeded row
        probes[torch.randint(m, (1,), generator=gen, device=device)] = True
    cols = torch.randint(k, (m,), generator=gen, device=device)
    signs = torch.randint(2, (m,), generator=gen, device=device) * 2 - 1
    powers = torch.randint(3, 8, (m,), generator=gen, device=device)  # |entry| 8 to 128
    spike = torch.zeros_like(x).scatter_(1, cols[:, None], (signs * 2.0 ** powers).float()[:, None])
    x = torch.where(probes[:, None], spike, x)
    return {"x": x.to(torch.bfloat16), "config": {"m": m, "n": n, "k": k, "layer": layer}}


def ref_kernel(data, weights):
    """out = x @ W[:N]^T: bfloat16 for the BF16 projections, float32 for the router."""
    layer, n = data["config"]["layer"], data["config"]["n"]
    out = data["x"].double() @ weights[layer][:n].double().T
    return out.to(torch.float32 if layer in FP32_LAYERS else torch.bfloat16)


def probe_rows(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Indices of rows with exactly one nonzero entry."""
    return ((x != 0).sum(-1) == 1).nonzero().flatten()


def check_implementation(data, output, weights):
    """Relative L2 error within tol (REL_L2_TOL, or ROUTER_TOL for the router) over the whole
    output and within 5x tol per row (checks.compare); each probe row within PROBE_TOL."""
    tol = ROUTER_TOL if data["config"]["layer"] in FP32_LAYERS else REL_L2_TOL
    ref = ref_kernel(data, weights)
    ok, msg = compare(output, ref, tol)
    rows = probe_rows(data["x"])
    if not ok or not len(rows):
        return ok, msg
    diff = (output[rows].double() - ref[rows].double()).norm(dim=-1) / ref[rows].double().norm(dim=-1).clamp(min=1e-30)
    worst = int(diff.argmax())
    if float(diff[worst]) > PROBE_TOL:
        return False, (f"{msg}, but probe row {int(rows[worst])} (one nonzero input, so a weight column, exact"
                       f" with the weights as given) is off by {float(diff[worst]):.2e} > {PROBE_TOL:g}: are the weights"
                       " used at their own precision?")
    return True, f"{msg}; {len(rows)} probe rows exact to {float(diff.max()):.1e}"


def speed_of_light_ns(m: int, layer: str, hw: dict, **_) -> float:
    n, k = out_features(layer, m), LAYERS[layer][1]
    w_bytes = 4 if layer in FP32_LAYERS else 2
    bytes_moved = n * k * w_bytes + m * k * 2 + m * n * w_bytes
    flops = 2.0 * m * n * k
    return 1e9 * max(bytes_moved / hw["hbm_bytes_per_s"], flops / hw["bf16_dense_flops_per_s"])
files.template.py:
"""Starter: the projections in plain PyTorch, correct but slow.

Implement kernel_fn, and prepare to repack the weights (called once, untimed)."""

from typing import TypedDict

import torch


class Weights(TypedDict):
    qkv_gate: torch.Tensor  # bfloat16 [2304, 8192]
    o: torch.Tensor         # bfloat16 [8192, 1024]
    pooler: torch.Tensor    # bfloat16 [4096, 8192]
    unpooler: torch.Tensor  # bfloat16 [8192, 4096]
    router: torch.Tensor    # float32 [256, 8192]


class Config(TypedDict):
    m: int
    n: int      # output width; the unpooler's is 1024 up to 8 tokens (this GPU's slice), else 8192
    k: int
    layer: str  # which weight: "qkv_gate", "o", "pooler", "unpooler" or "router"


class Inputs(TypedDict):
    x: torch.Tensor  # bfloat16 [m, k]
    config: Config


def prepare(weights: Weights) -> Weights:
    """Called once, untimed, before any case. Repack the weights as you like."""
    return weights


def kernel_fn(data: Inputs, weights: Weights) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Return x @ W[:n].T, where W is weights[config["layer"]]: bfloat16, or float32 for the router."""
    w = weights[data["config"]["layer"]][: data["config"]["n"]]
    if w.dtype == torch.float32:
        return data["x"].float() @ w.T
    return data["x"] @ w.T

task_md:
# Dense projections (`muse_bf16_proj`)

The attention and MoE-block projections and the router, as one GPU runs them serving Muse Spark Open on 8×H200. They are BF16 (the router FP32).

Your job is to compute this faster than SGLang's kernel does. Beside this file, `okc init` wrote:

- `submission.py`, your kernel. It starts as a plain PyTorch version of the computation. Keep its first line, `# okc: problem=muse_bf16_proj`: it tells `okc submit` the problem.
- `baseline.py`, SGLang's kernel: the one you're timed against.
- `reference.py`, the computation as the judge checks it: `generate_input`, the reference and the correctness checks, with `checks.py` beside it: the spec your output must meet. The judge uses its own copies, and runs them with steps of its own (the weights, routing fields, fresh inputs), so to check a change, use `okc check`.
- `AGENTS.md`, notes for a coding agent, if you use one.

## What to compute

```python
# x: [m, k] BF16   W: [n, k] = weights[layer]
# qkv_gate, o, pooler, unpooler: BF16; router: FP32
out = x @ W.T  # [m, n], BF16 (router: FP32)
```

`kernel_fn(data, state)` is the timed call and returns bfloat16 / float32 [m, n]. `state` is whatever `prepare(weights)` returned: it runs once, untimed, for up to 300 s. The `Inputs`, `Config` and `Weights` classes in submission.py give every field's dtype and shape; return GPU tensors of exactly that shape and dtype.

## Shapes

- m is the tokens per step: 1, 16 and 32 for decode, and 8, 128 and 256 for 8-token verify blocks. The weights arrive once, in prepare(), untimed.
- Decode loads are SGLang serving with speculative decoding off; verify loads are its default recipe, which checks each request's 8-token draft in one step.

| load | shape | weight | floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| decode 1 | m 1, layer qkv_gate | 62 | 7.9 µs |
| decode 1 | m 1, layer o | 62 | 3.5 µs |
| decode 1 | m 1, layer pooler | 62 | 14.0 µs |
| decode 1 | m 1, layer unpooler | 62 | 1.7 µs |
| decode 1 | m 1, layer router | 62 | 1.8 µs |
| decode 16 | m 16, layer qkv_gate | 62 | 7.9 µs |
| decode 16 | m 16, layer o | 62 | 3.6 µs |
| decode 16 | m 16, layer pooler | 62 | 14.1 µs |
| decode 16 | m 16, layer unpooler | 62 | 14.1 µs |
| decode 16 | m 16, layer router | 62 | 1.8 µs |
| decode 32 | m 32, layer qkv_gate | 62 | 8.0 µs |
| decode 32 | m 32, layer o | 62 | 3.6 µs |
| decode 32 | m 32, layer pooler | 62 | 14.1 µs |
| decode 32 | m 32, layer unpooler | 62 | 14.1 µs |
| decode 32 | m 32, layer router | 62 | 1.9 µs |
| verify 1 | m 8, layer qkv_gate | 62 | 7.9 µs |
| verify 1 | m 8, layer o | 62 | 3.5 µs |
| verify 1 | m 8, layer pooler | 62 | 14.0 µs |
| verify 1 | m 8, layer unpooler | 62 | 1.8 µs |
| verify 1 | m 8, layer router | 62 | 1.8 µs |
| verify 16 | m 128, layer qkv_gate | 62 | 8.4 µs |
| verify 16 | m 128, layer o | 62 | 4.0 µs |
| verify 16 | m 128, layer pooler | 62 | 14.6 µs |
| verify 16 | m 128, layer unpooler | 62 | 14.6 µs |
| verify 16 | m 128, layer router | 62 | 2.2 µs |
| verify 32 | m 256, layer qkv_gate | 62 | 9.8 µs |
| verify 32 | m 256, layer o | 62 | 4.5 µs |
| verify 32 | m 256, layer pooler | 62 | 17.4 µs |
| verify 32 | m 256, layer unpooler | 62 | 17.4 µs |
| verify 32 | m 256, layer router | 62 | 2.7 µs |

A shape's weight is how many times one step runs it. A load's time is the sum of its shapes' times, each times its weight. Your speedup on the problem is the geometric mean, over loads, of SGLang's load time over yours, so each load counts equally. The time shown for a run is SGLang's time per step, averaged over loads the same way, divided by that speedup.

The floor is the time to move the data at 4.8 TB/s or do the math at 989 TFLOP/s, whichever is longer.

Before timing, a run must pass these 9 tests, some harder than the scored shapes:

```
m 1, layer qkv_gate
m 7, layer pooler
m 33, layer o
m 130, layer unpooler
m 5, layer unpooler
m 8, layer router
m 9, layer router, dist outliers
m 512, layer qkv_gate, dist outliers
m 1000, layer unpooler, dist outliers
```

## Correctness

Every test and every timed call is checked against a reference. Errors are relative L2, |out − ref| / |ref|:

- The output, against an FP64 reference: at most 1%, and 0.01% for the router, whose outputs choose the experts. Splitting the router's FP32 weights into a BF16 hi + lo pair with FP32 accumulation, as SGLang does above 8 tokens, passes at any m; BF16 router weights alone don't.
- Use the weights at their own precision (the router's hi + lo split aside). About one row in eight of x has a single nonzero entry, a power of two, so its output is a column of the weights, exact with the original weights and slightly off with the router's hi + lo split. Those rows must be within 0.1%.
- Any single row: at most 5× its bound. A near-zero row is measured against a tenth of the average row.
- No NaN or Inf.

## How a run is timed

- Each shape is captured as a CUDA graph and timed by replaying it, in the same run and on the same GPU as SGLang's kernel, your replays and SGLang's taking turns on the same fresh inputs.
- Every timed replay starts with a cold L2: the judge reads a buffer larger than L2 just before it.
- A shape's speedup is the median of paired ratios: each repetition's SGLang time over yours, taken two repetitions at a time with the order swapped, so which side went first cancels. Your time on the shape is SGLang's median time over that speedup.
- Each run reports its speedup with a 95% interval (at least ±1.5%). Gains inside the interval might be noise.
- The judge subtracts a graph replay's fixed cost (about 4 µs) from both sides.

## Rules

- **CUDA graphs.** The timed calls replay `kernel_fn` as a CUDA graph: no host syncs (`.item()`, `.cpu()`, `torch.cuda.synchronize()`, printing a tensor), and no allocating or branching on input values. Branching on shapes and `config` is fine.
- **Fresh inputs.** Every call gets new inputs; don't cache anything derived from `data`.
- **Weights.** Repack them in `prepare()`, and compress them losslessly if you like, but don't store them at a different precision: NVFP4 weights stay NVFP4 and BF16 weights stay BF16, or smaller, losslessly. Dequantizing inside your kernels is fine. The router's FP32 weights may run as a BF16 hi + lo pair with FP32 accumulation, as SGLang does above 8 tokens.
- **Activations.** BF16 wherever SGLang's kernel keeps BF16.
- **Checked before running.** A submission is rejected if it patches timing, reads harness frames, touches harness I/O or secrets, edits loaded modules, imports the reference, starts processes or uses the network.

Full rules: https://openkernelchallenge.dev/rules

## Submitting

```bash
okc submit submission.py      # the tests, then timing; waits for the result
okc check submission.py       # the same run, kept off the board
okc status <job>              # a run's result again
okc jobs                      # your recent runs
```

A failing run names its first failing case and why. A passing run shows each shape's time against SGLang's and your speedup, and okc saves a profile beside your file, in `profiles/submission.<job>.txt`, showing where the time goes.

`print()` is fine for diagnostics (just not a tensor's values inside `kernel_fn`, which syncs). The last 16,000 characters of what a run prints come back with it, passing or not: okc saves it to `profiles/submission.<job>.log`, and `okc status <job> --json` has it as `log_tail`.

Runs on this problem have a daily limit, and the same code again returns its earlier result. `okc withdraw <job>` takes a run off the board. A check run (`okc check`) is the same run kept off the board and out of your attempts, for experiments, with a daily limit of its own. `okc problems` shows today's limits and what you have left; they reset at 00:00 UTC.

A run has 10 minutes in all, compiling included; one that runs past that is charged as a timeout.

## Where you stand

```bash
okc leaderboard muse_bf16_proj
```

Your best run is your row on the board, which is on the site too, at https://openkernelchallenge.dev/problems/muse_bf16_proj. It also counts toward the overall kernel board (`okc leaderboard`), which ranks by how much your best runs together would speed up a decode step.
